title: The potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1–6)
hook: clay spoiled on the wheel is shaped again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah threw out wisdom, might and riches as things to brag about, and kept kindness. Your line was here, in kitchens and courts and streets. Whose kindness did you tell? Today, the prophet goes to work, in someone else's workshop. Day eight hundred two.
screen: `HERE, IN KITCHENS AND COURTS AND STREETS.`

segments.voice: "Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words." This time the message doesn't come in a vision or a dream. Jeremiah is sent on an errand, down to a workshop. He goes, and there's the potter, working a lump of clay at the wheel. Wet hands, a turning wheel, a pot rising. And then, halfway up, something goes wrong. In a pottery class it looks like this: a wobble, a slump, a wall caving in. What the potter does next is the whole lesson.
screen: `GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.` → `A POT RISING ON THE WHEEL.` → `SOMETHING GOES WRONG.`

segments.voice: Here's what Jeremiah sees. "And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it." Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't throw the clay out. He doesn't sweep it off the wheel into the trash. The spoiled pot is still soft clay, and soft clay can be pressed back down and raised again into something else. Then the word comes. "O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter?" And: "Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand." On its own, that line could sound like a threat: you're just clay, and I can crush you. But read on, into the next verses. God says that if a nation he has spoken against turns from its evil, he will relent of the evil he planned for it. And if a nation he planned to build turns to evil, the plan can change too. The potter image is about turning. A vessel that's still on the wheel isn't finished. Mistakes don't end it; they're the reason the potter's hands go back to work. Jewish tradition carries this picture into Yom Kippur. In the Ashkenazi evening service, a liturgical poem built on Jeremiah's image is sung: behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are we in your hand. On the night of turning, the people call themselves clay that can still be reshaped.
screen: `THE VESSEL WAS MARRED.` · `HE MADE IT AGAIN.` · then, large: `AS CLAY IN THE POTTER'S HAND.` · then: `CLAY ON THE WHEEL CAN TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let yourself be reshaped. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place in your life that feels marred, a habit that slumped, a plan that caved in, a way you've been treating someone. Don't throw it away in your mind, and don't defend it either. Just hold it the way a potter holds soft clay. Ask: what could this become, if it were pressed down and raised again? Let one small new shape come. Then breathe out, and let your hands, your shoulders, your jaw go soft, like clay that can still move. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur, the night of turning, when a liturgical poem sung in the Ashkenazi evening service borrows Jeremiah's image: as clay in the hand of the potter, so are we in your hand. Today's word.
Your line: as clay in his hand. Today, when something you made goes wrong, don't throw it out; press it down and try again. Day eight hundred two.

howItsDone: On Yom Kippur evening, Ashkenazi prayer books include the liturgical poem Ki hineh kachomer, behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, which takes its image from Jeremiah 18.

original.note: Hebrew: as the clay in the potter's hand, from Jeremiah 18:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: God can crush us like clay.
what it means: a marred pot still on the wheel is made again; the image is about turning and being reshaped.
what a scholar hears: the next verses (18:7–10) say a nation that turns from evil can see God relent, and Yom Kippur's Ki hineh kachomer sings the image.
